Part-DINO: Complementing DINO Features with Image Structure for Part Discovery

AbstractInsightsMethodResultsCitation

Abstract

Self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs) like DINO encode rich semantics, enabling training-free segmentation of objects from the background and discovery of their parts via feature clustering. This paper focuses on part discovery: partitioning a foreground object into semantic parts. Existing approaches produce imprecise part boundaries. We trace this to the rigid ViT patch grid used in training DINO, where patches straddling boundaries contain pixels from multiple parts. While DINO’s invariance-based training could absorb this pixel-level mixing into clean features, experiments with over 26K foreground patches show it does not: boundary-overlapping patches produce features with higher entropy and lower assignment confidence, blurring predicted part boundaries.

Rather than make the massive effort of retraining DINO over geometrically coherent regions, an easier approach is to take boundaries directly from a boundary detector, which supplies the geometric information DINO’s features lack.

Motivated by this, we introduce Part-DINO, a training-free framework that combines boundaries from low-level image segmentation with DINO’s semantic features. We use the boundaries to partition the image into regions, pool DINO features within each region, and group them to discover parts. Without any training, Part-DINO produces structurally coherent part assignments, outperforming training-free baselines across four standard benchmarks (CUB, CelebA, PartImageNet-OOD, PartImageNet-Seg) and remaining competitive with weakly-supervised and unsupervised methods.

Why Do Part Boundaries Blur?

A fixed square patch can cross the boundary between two parts, mixing their pixels before feature extraction. We find that this mixing remains in DINO’s features, making part assignments less reliable near boundaries.

Pixel Mixing Propagates into Feature Space

Across 26,459 foreground patches from PartImageNet, patches closer to a ground-truth part boundary have lower spatial purity, higher feature entropy, and a smaller gap between their two strongest part assignments. 21.9% of the foreground patches contain pixels from more than one part.

The Part-DINO Method

Part-DINO combines boundaries from low-level image segmentation with semantic features from a frozen DINO encoder. Regions replace square patches as the units of part discovery.

  1. Generate regions from image structure. Within a foreground mask, the RAMP transform estimates local intensity contrast. Watershed partitions this edge map into regions along its ridges.
  2. Build global part prototypes. We upsample frozen DINO features, pool them within each region, and apply K-means to region features from reference images. The K cluster centers represent parts shared across object instances.
  3. Assign regions to parts. For a new image, each region receives the label of its most similar part prototype under cosine similarity. All pixels in a region share the same label.
Implementation details and optional region merging

Experiments use frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 with registers and SAM3 foreground masks. Input resolution is 448 × 448 for CUB and 224 × 224 for the other datasets. RAMP uses four orientations, and watershed seeds have a minimum spacing of 2 pixels.

The default pipeline merges micro-regions smaller than 10 pixels into their most similar adjacent region using DINO cosine similarity. This step only removes existing boundaries; it does not introduce new boundaries. Setting the minimum region size to zero disables merging, leaving the RAMP + watershed partition unchanged.

“Training-free” means no dataset-specific neural-network optimization: the encoder stays frozen, while part prototypes are obtained through clustering. For multi-category datasets, the method maintains a separate part dictionary per category and selects the category using CLS-feature similarity.

Results

We evaluate on CUB, CelebA, PartImageNet-OOD, and PartImageNet-Seg. Part-DINO improves ARI over the foreground-matched patch baseline at every evaluated part granularity on all four benchmarks. It also improves NME on CUB and CelebA, and NMI on three of the four benchmarks.

CUB at K = 16

Against the DINO + SAM patch baseline, NMI increases from 56.92 to 65.45 (+8.53 points), ARI from 35.10 to 46.00 (+10.90 points), and NME decreases from 4.87 to 4.35.
